# Acts of Thomas — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (possibly from the school of Bardaisan in Edessa, Syria) |
| **Date** | c. 200–250 CE |
| **Audience** | Syriac-speaking Eastern Christians; possibly Encratite (ascetic) communities |
| **Genre** | Apostolic romance / travel narrative / aretalogy (account of wonders) |
| **Timeline** | Early third century; likely composed in Syriac with Greek translation following |
| **In One Sentence** | The story of the apostle Thomas sold as a slave and carried to India, where he converts a king and a nobleman, performs astonishing miracles, preaches radical sexual renunciation, and is martyred — containing within it the Hymn of the Pearl, one of the most beautiful poems in all of early Christian literature. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Acts of Thomas is one of five major Apocryphal Acts (alongside the Acts of Peter, Paul, Andrew, and John) that circulated widely in the early centuries as extended narratives of the apostles' post-resurrection missions. Like the others, it combines novelistic adventure, miraculous wonder-working, and theological teaching — it is popular Christian literature in the fullest sense, designed for wide audiences who wanted exciting narrative alongside spiritual instruction.

The text was almost certainly originally composed in Syriac, the Aramaic dialect spoken in the region around Edessa (modern Urfa in Turkey), which was the heartland of Eastern Syrian Christianity. The Syriac and Greek versions both survive, and scholars disagree about which is primary — though the current consensus leans toward Syriac. The difference matters theologically: the Syriac version is more consistently Encratite (the Greek word for "self-controlled" — a radical ascetic movement that viewed all sexual activity, even within marriage, as spiritually harmful), while the Greek version softens some of the more extreme passages.

The Indian setting is not fantasy. The Thomas tradition — that the apostle Thomas traveled to India and founded Christianity there — is taken as historical fact by the Thomas Christians of Kerala (southwestern India), who trace their community back to Thomas's missionary work in the first century CE. Whether this tradition has any historical basis is debated, but the Indian details in the Acts (including the historically attested King Gundaphorus/Gondophares, who ruled parts of northwestern India in the first century CE) suggest real contact with the Indian world.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Acts of Thomas serves multiple purposes simultaneously. At the narrative level, it is an entertaining adventure story — Thomas is sold by Jesus (his twin) to an Indian merchant, travels to India, builds a palace that turns out to be in heaven rather than on earth, moves to another kingdom, works miracles, converts noblemen and their wives, and eventually faces martyrdom. The story is episodic, vivid, and designed for oral performance and recitation in Christian communities.

At the theological level, the Acts of Thomas is a sustained argument for radical sexual renunciation as the true Christian life. Every conversion Thomas achieves involves the converted person renouncing their marriage bed — including, most dramatically, a newly married couple (the Bridal Chamber scene, Act 1) who are converted on their wedding night and choose perpetual continence. This is not presented as exceptional asceticism but as the normal consequence of receiving the Holy Spirit and recognizing the true nature of the material world. The wedding hymn sung at the bridal chamber scene (chapters 6–7) — addressed to the divine Sophia and her bridegroom — is itself one of the most beautiful poetic passages in the text.

The Hymn of the Pearl (chapters 108–113) is the text's literary and theological summit. Embedded in a prayer that Thomas offers in prison, it is a complete allegorical poem about a prince sent from his heavenly home to Egypt to retrieve a pearl, who falls asleep and forgets his origin, is awakened by a letter from his divine parents, retrieves the pearl, and returns home. The allegory maps onto the Gnostic/Sethian anthropological myth — the soul, divine in origin, fallen into the material world (Egypt), forgetful of its true nature, awakened by divine revelation, and returning to its source. Whether the Hymn was composed for the Acts or was an originally independent poem incorporated into it is debated, but it stands on its own as one of the greatest early Christian poems.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Acts of Thomas is long (about 170 chapters) and should be read in selected sections unless you are committed to the whole. Essential reading includes:

Act 1 (chapters 1–16): The divine lottery in which the apostles divide the world's mission territories. Thomas refuses India; Jesus appears and sells him as a slave to Abbanes, an Indian merchant. The wedding night at the bridal chamber, the wedding hymn to Sophia, and the newly married couple's decision for continence.

Act 2 (chapters 17–29): Thomas in India with King Gundaphorus. He is given money to build a palace and instead distributes it to the poor, telling Gundaphorus that he has built a palace — in heaven. The king is furious until his recently dead brother returns from the afterlife and reports having seen the glorious heavenly palace Thomas built.

The Anaphora of Thomas (chapters 26–27): One of the most beautiful early Eucharistic prayers, addressed to Jesus under multiple titles — "Jesus Christ, the compassion of the Father and perfect hope, the deliverer of the oppressed and redeemer of souls." It is a breathtaking piece of liturgical prose.

The Hymn of the Pearl (chapters 108–113): Read this slowly and several times. The prince's letter from his parents has one of the most tender moments in all of early Christian literature: "Awake and rise up out of sleep, and give ear to the words of our letter. Remember that you are a king's son; look at the slavery you are serving. Remember the pearl for the sake of which you did journey to Egypt." After reading the Acts of Thomas as a whole, come back to the Hymn and you will see how perfectly it maps onto Thomas's own story — and onto the reader's story.

The martyrdom (chapters 160–170): Thomas is killed by the Indian king Misdaeus (whose wife and son Thomas had converted to continence). His death is serene and voluntary — the true martyr's death of someone who has long since ceased to fear the destruction of a body he regards as temporary clothing.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The Hymn of the Pearl connects the Acts of Thomas to the broader Gnostic tradition of the soul's fall and return, to the Hellenistic philosophical tradition of the soul's imprisonment in matter (Plato's Phaedo, Plotinus's Enneads), and to the Odes of Solomon (the greatest collection of early Syriac Christian poetry, probably also from Edessa). The Hymn is widely considered the finest artistic expression of this theological myth.

The Thomas-as-twin-of-Jesus motif connects to the Gospel of Thomas (the opening of which identifies its author as "Didymus Judas Thomas") and to the Book of Thomas the Contender. In all of these texts, Thomas's unique qualification to transmit Jesus's teaching is his identity as Jesus's twin — not necessarily biological, but metaphysical, as the disciple who most perfectly mirrors and understands his master.

The Indian Christian tradition connects to a historical reality. The Thomas Christians of Kerala (the Nasrani or Saint Thomas Christians) are one of the oldest Christian communities in the world. They claim Thomas arrived in Kerala in 52 CE, founded seven churches, and was martyred at Mylapore (modern Chennai) in 72 CE. Archaeological evidence is sparse but not absent — and the fact that the Acts names King Gundaphorus, who is historically attested in numismatic and inscriptional evidence from the region (modern Pakistan/Afghanistan) in roughly the first century CE, suggests real historical contact between early Christianity and the Indian subcontinent.

The Encratite theology of the Acts connects to Tatian (a second-century Syrian Christian apologist who became associated with extreme asceticism), to Marcion's church (which rejected marriage and meat), and to the broader phenomenon of ascetic Christianity that would eventually give rise to Christian monasticism.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The Encratite sexual ethic will be deeply alien — and troubling — to most modern readers. The Acts of Thomas does not merely promote celibacy as a higher calling for those gifted with it (as in Paul's 1 Corinthians 7: "it is better not to marry" for those who can bear it). It presents sexual renunciation as the condition of salvation and marriage as a trap. Wives who convert to Thomas's teaching and withhold themselves from their husbands are presented as heroes; husbands who consequently plot Thomas's death are presented as victims of their own spiritual blindness. This is not Paul — it is a Christianity in which the body's reproductive functions are themselves evidence of the Fall.

This matters because it represents a real and widespread strain of early Christianity that was eventually condemned as heresy (Encratism was condemned by multiple councils) but was enormously influential before its condemnation. The asceticism of Christian monasticism, the valorization of perpetual virginity, the ambivalence toward marriage in much of early Christian thought — all of these have roots in the Encratite impulse, even after the extreme Encratite position was rejected.

The divine lottery (Act 1) in which the apostles divide the world's territories is itself a wonderful piece of early Christian imaginative geography — a moment where we see how early Christians conceptualized the scope of the apostolic mission as genuinely global, extending even to the mysterious lands at the edge of the known world (India = the far East in Mediterranean imagination).

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Acts of Thomas was explicitly excluded from serious canonical consideration because of its Encratite theology and its attribution to a non-apostolic anonymous author presenting heterodox content under apostolic cover. The Manichaeans (a syncretic religious movement that drew heavily on Gnostic Christianity) used the Acts of Thomas extensively, which further damaged its reputation in mainstream Christian circles.

Eusebius does not include it in his canonical discussions — it was simply not in the running. Augustine attacked the Manichaeans for their use of the Apocryphal Acts. The Gelasian Decree (a fifth- or sixth-century canonical document) explicitly listed the Acts of Thomas among apocryphal and rejected texts.

The text nevertheless remained in wide use in the East, particularly in the Syriac-speaking church, where the Thomas tradition was central to Christian identity. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, with its broader canon, has ties to the Eastern tradition of revering Thomas. The Indian Thomas Christians have always honored the Acts of Thomas as a treasured (if not canonical) account of their founding. Today the text is studied as a crucial witness to early Eastern Christianity, Encratite theology, and the surprisingly wide geographical imagination of second-century Christian mission.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 20–46 CE | Reign of Gondophares/Gundaphorus in northwestern India (historical) |
| c. 52 CE | Traditional date of Thomas's arrival in India (per Indian Christian tradition) |
| c. 72 CE | Traditional date of Thomas's martyrdom at Mylapore |
| c. 200–250 CE | Acts of Thomas composed, probably in Syriac at Edessa |
| c. 200–300 CE | Greek translation made; text circulates widely |
| c. 250–350 CE | Manichaeans adopt and promote the text |
| c. 400 CE | Augustine attacks Manichaean use of Apocryphal Acts |
| c. 496 CE | Gelasian Decree lists Acts of Thomas among rejected texts |
| 1823 CE | First critical edition of the Greek text |
| 1871 CE | William Wright publishes Syriac text |
| 1936 CE | Standard critical edition by A.F.J. Klijn |

---
